Why Disability-Inclusive Economic Participation Matters

Persons with disabilities can encounter multiple barriers to education, skills development, employment and entrepreneurship.

These barriers may occur at different levels, including within communities, educational institutions, workplaces, public institutions and labour markets.

A disability-inclusive economic empowerment project can therefore address several interconnected challenges at the same time.

For example, a project could combine skills development with employer engagement, accessibility improvements, entrepreneurship support and awareness activities.

This type of integrated approach can help move beyond simply identifying barriers and instead create practical pathways towards greater participation.

How Organisations Can Strengthen Their Proposals

Organisations preparing an application should ensure that their proposed project is directly connected to the objectives of the call.

Demonstrate a Clearly Defined Problem

Avoid describing disability exclusion only in general terms.

Explain the specific problem affecting the target community and provide evidence wherever possible.

Identify Specific Beneficiaries

Clearly explain who will benefit, including relevant characteristics such as location, disability-related needs and economic circumstances where appropriate.

Provide Measurable Results

Instead of saying that the project will “empower persons with disabilities,” explain what measurable changes the project expects to achieve.

For example, the proposal could establish measurable targets relating to skills acquisition, employment pathways, entrepreneurship, accessibility improvements or institutional capacity.

Build Relevant Partnerships

Projects can involve employers, disability organisations, government institutions, training institutions, private companies and other stakeholders.

Clearly define what each partner will contribute.

Develop a Realistic Budget

The proposed expenditure should correspond directly with the project’s activities and expected results.

Applicants should pay particular attention to the 7% equipment limit and 8% administrative/operational cost limit.

Demonstrate Sustainability

Explain how the project’s benefits can continue after the 12-month grant period.

Sustainability could involve institutional partnerships, employer relationships, community ownership, income-generating mechanisms, capacity building or integration into existing systems.

Deadline for the 2026 Dwabo Small Grants Programme

The application deadline is

23 September 2026 at 23:59

Both the hard-copy and electronic application requirements should be completed by the deadline.

Because the deadline is approaching, eligible organisations should begin preparing the application, supporting documents and budget as early as possible.

Visit HERE for more information about the 2026 Dwabo Small Grants Programme in Ghana.

Conclusion

The 2026 Dwabo Small Grants Programme provides an opportunity for eligible civil society organisations in Ghana to secure funding for practical projects aimed at advancing the economic inclusion, employability and meaningful participation of persons with disabilities.

With grants of €8,000 to €10,000 available for projects lasting 12 months, the programme is particularly relevant to organisations working in disability inclusion, skills development, employment, entrepreneurship, livelihoods, accessibility, education and human rights.

The call places strong emphasis on locally grounded and measurable interventions. Applicants should therefore develop proposals that clearly identify a specific problem, define their beneficiaries, present practical solutions, establish measurable indicators and demonstrate appropriate organisational and financial capacity.

Organisations should also carefully follow the financial and administrative requirements, including the minimum 10% co-financing requirement, the 8% ceiling for administrative and operational costs, the 7% limit on equipment expenditure, and the requirement for both hard-copy and electronic submission.

Eligible organisations should review the official 2026 Terms of Reference and application documents carefully and submit their complete applications before 23 September 2026 at 23:59.

item.content:encoded:
Stanford University’s Walter H. Shorenstein Asia-Pacific Research Center (APARC) is inviting applications for several fellowship opportunities beginning in Fall Quarter 2027. These fellowships are designed for scholars, researchers, academics, and professionals interested in contemporary Asia and provide opportunities to conduct research, develop academic work, engage with other scholars, and contribute to research on major political, economic, social, health, and policy issues affecting the Asia-Pacific region.

The 2027–2028 fellowship cycle includes opportunities covering contemporary Asia broadly, Asia health policy, Southeast Asia, Taiwan, and emerging policy challenges across Asia. Several opportunities are specifically designed for recent PhD recipients, while others are available to mid-career, senior, or established scholars and professionals.

With different eligibility requirements, research areas, fellowship durations, and deadlines, applicants should carefully identify the fellowship that best matches their academic background and research interests.

About Stanford APARC

The Walter H. Shorenstein Asia-Pacific Research Center (APARC) at Stanford University is a research and education center focused on contemporary Asia and the Asia-Pacific region.

Through its research programs, APARC provides opportunities for scholars and researchers to investigate important developments across the region, including political and economic change, healthcare policy, international relations, social issues, technology, development, and regional policy challenges.

For the 2027–2028 academic year, APARC is offering several fellowship opportunities through its different research programs.

These include:

  1. Shorenstein Postdoctoral Fellowship on Contemporary Asia
  2. Asia Health Policy Program Postdoctoral Fellowship
  3. Lee Kong Chian NUS-Stanford Fellowship on Southeast Asia
  4. Stanford Next Asia Policy Lab Postdoctoral and Visiting Fellowships
  5. Taiwan Program Kwoh-Ting Li Visiting Fellowship

Each fellowship has its own research focus and eligibility requirements.

APPLY HERE

1. 2027–2028 Shorenstein Postdoctoral Fellowship on Contemporary Asia

The Shorenstein Postdoctoral Fellowship on Contemporary Asia provides an opportunity for recent PhD recipients to undertake research focused broadly on contemporary Asia.

APARC is offering two postdoctoral fellowship positions for the 2027–2028 academic year.

Research areas

The fellowship broadly focuses on research examining important developments in the Asia-Pacific region.

Research may address:

  • Political change
  • Economic change
  • Social change
  • International relations
  • International political economy

The geographical scope is broad and includes:

  • Northeast Asia
  • Southeast Asia
  • South Asia
  • The wider Asia-Pacific region

This makes the fellowship potentially relevant to researchers examining contemporary political, economic, and social developments across different parts of Asia.

Fellowship duration

Appointments are for one academic year.

The fellowship is scheduled to begin in Fall Quarter 2027.

Number of positions

There are two postdoctoral fellowship positions available.

Deadline

December 1, 2026

Application

Applicants interested in the Shorenstein Postdoctoral Fellowship should review the specific application requirements and submit their application through the Stanford APARC fellowship process.

2. 2027–2028 Asia Health Policy Program Postdoctoral Fellowship

The Asia Health Policy Program Postdoctoral Fellowship is offered through APARC’s Asia Health Policy Program.

This fellowship is specifically designed for research concerning contemporary health or healthcare policy in the Asia-Pacific region.

One fellowship position is available for a recent PhD recipient.

Research focus

The fellowship supports research on health and healthcare policy issues that have significant relevance to countries in the Asia-Pacific region.

Particular attention is given to issues relevant to developing countries in the region.

Potential research can therefore examine contemporary questions surrounding healthcare systems, health policy, and related challenges affecting Asian countries.

Fellowship duration

The appointment lasts for one academic year.

It begins in Fall Quarter 2027.

Number of positions

One postdoctoral fellowship position is available.

Who is this opportunity particularly relevant to?

This fellowship is particularly relevant to researchers whose academic work focuses on:

  • Health policy
  • Healthcare policy
  • Health systems
  • Contemporary Asian health issues
  • Policy challenges affecting developing countries in Asia-Pacific

Deadline

December 1, 2026

Applicants should consult the fellowship’s specific application page for the complete requirements.

3. 2027–2028 Lee Kong Chian NUS-Stanford Fellowship on Southeast Asia

The Lee Kong Chian NUS-Stanford Fellowship on Southeast Asia supports scholarship and research concerning contemporary Southeast Asia.

Unlike the postdoctoral fellowships above, this opportunity is open to candidates at all career stages, provided they have professional backgrounds and ongoing positions in the social sciences or humanities.

Research focus

The fellowship is focused specifically on contemporary Southeast Asia.

Researchers can use the fellowship period to pursue:

  • Research projects
  • Scholarly writing
  • Academic investigation
  • Projects related to contemporary Southeast Asian issues

The fellowship is supported by APARC’s Southeast Asia Program.

Fellowship duration

Lee Kong Chian Fellows spend approximately two to three quarters at Stanford pursuing their research and writing projects.

Appointments must both begin and conclude within the period:

September 1, 2027 – June 30, 2028

Career stage

A major feature of this fellowship is that it is not restricted to recent PhD recipients.

It is open to candidates at all career stages who meet the specified professional and academic requirements.

Important change to the fellowship

The announcement notes an important change to the programme.

The fellowship is no longer offered as a joint-residency programme with the National University of Singapore (NUS).

Fellows appointed through Stanford will be hosted at Stanford’s Asia-Pacific Research Center, while fellows appointed through NUS will be hosted at NUS.

Applicants who specifically want to pursue the fellowship at NUS should apply through the NUS application portal.

Deadline

January 25, 2027

4. Stanford Next Asia Policy Lab Postdoctoral and Visiting Fellowships

The Stanford Next Asia Policy Lab (SNAPL) is another research programme housed at APARC.

SNAPL focuses on emerging social, cultural, economic, and political challenges affecting Asia.

The lab is led by Korea Program Director Gi-Wook Shin and focuses on four major research themes:

  1. Talent Flows and Development
  2. Nationalism and Racism
  3. U.S.-Asia Relations
  4. Democratic Crisis and Reform

For the 2027–2028 fellowship cycle, SNAPL is offering three different fellowship opportunities.

I. 2027–2029 Next Asia Policy Postdoctoral Fellowship

The Next Asia Policy Postdoctoral Fellowship provides opportunities for recent PhD recipients to conduct research related to any of SNAPL’s four research tracks.

Research tracks

Applicants may develop research related to:

  • Talent Flows and Development
  • Nationalism and Racism
  • U.S.-Asia Relations
  • Democratic Crisis and Reform

Number of positions

SNAPL is offering two positions.

Fellowship duration

The appointments begin in Fall Quarter 2027 and last for two years.

An extension may be possible depending on:

  • Satisfactory performance
  • Available funding

Eligibility focus

This opportunity is intended for recent PhD recipients whose research aligns with one or more of SNAPL’s research themes.

Deadline

December 1, 2026

II. 2027–2028 STINT-SNAPL Postdoctoral Fellowship

The STINT-SNAPL Postdoctoral Fellowship is offered jointly with the Swedish Foundation for International Cooperation in Research and Higher Education (STINT).

The fellowship provides one position for a recent PhD recipient.

Research focus

The fellowship focuses on:

  • Scientific policy
  • Internationalization of higher education
  • Internationalization of research
  • The Asia-Pacific region

Preference is given to projects that directly or indirectly engage with Swedish perspectives.

This makes the opportunity particularly relevant to researchers examining how higher education and research systems interact internationally and how these issues relate to Asia-Pacific countries.

Fellowship duration

The appointment:

  • Begins in Fall Quarter 2027
  • Runs for one year
  • May potentially be extended depending on satisfactory performance and available funding

Number of positions

One postdoctoral fellowship position is available.

Deadline

December 1, 2026

III. 2027–2028 Next Asia Policy Visiting Fellowship

The Next Asia Policy Visiting Fellowship is designed for researchers and professionals from the Asia-Pacific region.

Two visiting fellow positions are available.

Eligibility background

Applicants should:

  • Be researchers or professionals from the Asia-Pacific region
  • Hold a PhD, or
  • Have a substantial record of achievement related to one of SNAPL’s four research themes

Unlike the postdoctoral opportunities, this fellowship is therefore not limited exclusively to recent PhD recipients.

Research priority

For this fellowship cycle, SNAPL will prioritize scholars working on economic security.

One of the two visiting fellow positions is specifically dedicated to research concerning the Philippines.

Fellowship duration

Appointments:

  • Begin in Fall Quarter 2027
  • Last for one academic year

Deadline

March 1, 2027

5. 2027–2028 Taiwan Program Kwoh-Ting Li Visiting Fellowship

The Kwoh-Ting Li Visiting Fellowship is offered through APARC’s Taiwan Program.

It provides an opportunity for experienced scholars to conduct research and participate in academic activities related to contemporary Taiwan.

Who is the fellowship designed for?

The fellowship is open to:

  • Mid-career scholars in Taiwan studies
  • Senior scholars in Taiwan studies

The opportunity is therefore particularly suited to established researchers with a substantial academic background in Taiwan-related research.

Research areas

The fellowship supports research on contemporary Taiwan across a broad range of subjects.

These may include:

  • Taiwan’s economy
  • Taiwanese society
  • Demography
  • Environment
  • Technology
  • Other areas of contemporary Taiwan studies

Activities during the fellowship

The fellowship provides scholars with an opportunity to:

  • Conduct research
  • Write
  • Participate in seminars
  • Teach a course
  • Engage with academic activities at Stanford

Fellowship duration

The appointment:

  • Begins in Fall Quarter 2027
  • Runs for one academic year

Deadline

March 1, 2027

Fellowship Deadlines at a Glance

Applicants should pay close attention to the individual deadlines because the opportunities do not all close on the same date.

Fellowship Positions Duration Deadline
Shorenstein Postdoctoral Fellowship on Contemporary Asia 2 1 academic year December 1, 2026
Asia Health Policy Program Postdoctoral Fellowship 1 1 academic year December 1, 2026
Lee Kong Chian NUS-Stanford Fellowship on Southeast Asia Not specified in supplied announcement 2–3 quarters January 25, 2027
Next Asia Policy Postdoctoral Fellowship 2 2 years December 1, 2026
STINT-SNAPL Postdoctoral Fellowship 1 1 year December 1, 2026
Next Asia Policy Visiting Fellowship 2 1 academic year March 1, 2027
Kwoh-Ting Li Visiting Fellowship Not specified in supplied announcement 1 academic year March 1, 2027

Why These Fellowships Are Significant

The Stanford APARC fellowship programme brings together opportunities covering several major areas of contemporary Asian studies.

Depending on the fellowship, scholars can focus on issues such as:

  • Political transformation
  • Economic development
  • Social change
  • International relations
  • International political economy
  • Health policy
  • Healthcare systems
  • Southeast Asian studies
  • Higher education and research policy
  • Talent mobility
  • Nationalism
  • Racism
  • U.S.-Asia relations
  • Democratic challenges
  • Economic security
  • Taiwan’s economy and society
  • Technology
  • Demography
  • Environmental issues

The different programmes also accommodate different stages of an academic or professional career. Some opportunities specifically target recent PhD recipients, while others are available to researchers and professionals with established records of achievement.

Visit HERE to learn more about the Stanford APARC Fellowships 2027–2028

How to Choose the Appropriate Fellowship

Applicants should first identify their research topic, geographical focus, and career stage.

If your research covers contemporary Asia broadly

The Shorenstein Postdoctoral Fellowship may be relevant for recent PhD recipients researching political, economic, or social change, international relations, or international political economy in Asia.

If your research focuses on health

The Asia Health Policy Program Postdoctoral Fellowship is specifically focused on contemporary health and healthcare policy in the Asia-Pacific region.

If you study Southeast Asia

The Lee Kong Chian NUS-Stanford Fellowship is designed for scholarship concerning contemporary Southeast Asia and is open to candidates at all career stages who meet its professional requirements.

If your research fits emerging Asian policy challenges

The Stanford Next Asia Policy Lab fellowships provide opportunities across four research themes, including talent flows, nationalism and racism, U.S.-Asia relations, and democratic crisis and reform.

If your work focuses on Taiwan

The Kwoh-Ting Li Visiting Fellowship is designed for mid-career and senior scholars in Taiwan studies.

Important Considerations Before Applying

Because these are different fellowship programmes, applicants should not assume that meeting the requirements for one automatically means they qualify for all of them.

Before submitting an application, prospective applicants should:

  1. Identify the fellowship that corresponds to their research area.
  2. Check whether the opportunity is intended for recent PhD recipients, visiting researchers, or established scholars.
  3. Review the specific application requirements.
  4. Confirm the fellowship duration and expected start period.
  5. Prepare the required academic and research materials.
  6. Ensure that the research proposal or project aligns with the fellowship’s stated focus.
  7. Submit the application before the relevant deadline.

Applicants should also pay particular attention to the distinction between the Stanford-hosted Lee Kong Chian fellowship and the NUS application route, as the announcement states that applicants wishing to pursue the fellowship at NUS should apply through the NUS portal.

Conclusion

The Stanford APARC Fellowships 2027–2028 provide a range of research opportunities for scholars and researchers working on contemporary Asia. The fellowship portfolio covers broad regional research as well as specialized areas including health policy, Southeast Asia, Taiwan, higher education and research policy, economic security, international relations, political change, and social development.

The opportunities also differ considerably in terms of career stage. Recent PhD recipients can apply for several postdoctoral positions, while the Lee Kong Chian Fellowship welcomes candidates at all career stages, the Next Asia Policy Visiting Fellowship targets researchers and professionals from the Asia-Pacific region, and the Kwoh-Ting Li Fellowship is intended for mid-career and senior Taiwan scholars.

Applicants should therefore carefully match their academic background, career stage, geographical specialization, and research interests with the specific fellowship before applying. The earliest deadline among the listed opportunities is December 1, 2026, while other fellowships have deadlines in January and March 2027.

For more global grants, scholarships, fellowships, internships, jobs, conferences, competitions, and other career opportunities for young people, visit the Opportunities for Youth (OFY) website at www.opportunitiesforyouth.org.

item.content:encoded:
The Collections & Communities in the East of England Collaborative Doctoral Landscape Award (CC-EE) is inviting proposals for PhD studentship projects that use collections held by participating cultural and collecting institutions across the East of England.

The programme offers an opportunity for UK university-based academics and staff working within participating collections to develop collaborative doctoral research projects that connect collections with important contemporary and historical questions through arts and humanities methodologies.

For the 2027/28 academic year, the programme plans to allocate five studentships. Each successful PhD project will involve a partnership between at least two CC-EE collections and a UK university, creating a collaborative research environment in which doctoral students can work across institutional boundaries while gaining access to specialist training, research support and dedicated research funding.

The initiative is particularly interested in projects connected to the themes of belonging, resilience and ecologies, while allowing research to address a broad range of collections-related activities, including curatorial work, interpretation, learning and conservation.

Opportunity Overview

  • Opportunity: Collections & Communities in the East of England Collaborative Doctoral Landscape Award
  • Programme: Collections & Communities in the East of England (CC-EE)
  • Opportunity type: PhD studentship proposal / doctoral research opportunity
  • Studentships available: 5 for 2027/28
  • Expected PhD start: October 2027
  • Geographical focus: East of England
  • Participating collection locations: Cambridge, Norfolk, Colchester, Ipswich and Peterborough
  • Required methodology: Arts and humanities methods
  • Key themes: Belonging, resilience and ecologies
  • Expression of Interest deadline: 26 October 2026 at 12:00 noon
  • Full Application deadline: 16 December 2026 at 12:00 noon
  • Application process: Two-stage selection process

About the Collections & Communities in the East of England Programme

The Collections & Communities in the East of England initiative brings together collections and communities across the region with the aim of using collections-based research to engage with significant questions and challenges.

The programme is based around the idea that collections held by museums, archives, galleries and other cultural institutions can provide valuable material for doctoral research. These collections can support research into history, culture, society, heritage, communities, environments and numerous other areas within the arts and humanities.

The Collaborative Doctoral Landscape Award provides a structure through which universities and collection-holding institutions can work together to develop doctoral research projects.

Rather than limiting a PhD project to a single university or collection, each studentship is designed around a collaborative partnership involving two or more CC-EE collections and a UK university.

This structure allows doctoral researchers to engage directly with collections and the professionals who care for them while also benefiting from the academic environment and research expertise of a university.

Five PhD Studentships Available for 2027/28

The CC-EE programme plans to allocate five studentships for the 2027/28 academic year.

The resulting doctoral projects are expected to begin in October 2027.

An important feature of the programme is that the studentships themselves will be externally advertised. The current call is therefore focused on identifying and developing suitable doctoral research projects and supervisory partnerships rather than directly inviting individual prospective PhD students to apply for admission at this stage.

Successful proposals will subsequently form the basis for externally advertised PhD opportunities.

This makes the current call particularly relevant to academics and collection professionals who have a strong research idea and are interested in developing it into a collaborative doctoral project.

Where Can Proposed PhD Projects Be Based?

The programme is specifically interested in PhD projects that make use of collections located across the East of England.

The opportunity identifies collections in:

  • Cambridge
  • Norfolk
  • Colchester
  • Ipswich
  • Peterborough

The project must involve collaboration between at least two of the participating CC-EE collecting institutions, with the partnership also including a UK university.

Projects involving more than two collections are particularly welcomed.

This multi-institutional structure means that applicants should consider how collections held by different organisations can complement one another and contribute to a coherent doctoral research question.

What Types of Research Projects Are Eligible?

Proposed doctoral research should be based on collections held by participating CC-EE institutions and should employ arts and humanities methodologies.

The programme does not restrict research to a single discipline or one particular type of collections work. Instead, the call provides considerable scope for applicants to develop projects around different aspects of collection-based research.

Potential areas of research may include:

1. Curatorial Research

Projects can investigate how collections are understood, organised, interpreted and presented to the public.

A doctoral project could explore curatorial practices, the development of collections, changing interpretations of objects or materials, or how institutions make decisions about what and how collections are presented.

2. Interpretation

Research may focus on how collections are interpreted for different audiences.

This could include examining exhibitions, displays, interpretive materials, digital interpretation or other ways institutions communicate the significance of collections.

3. Learning and Education

Projects can also explore the relationship between collections and learning.

Research could investigate how museums, archives and other collecting institutions use their collections to support education, public learning, community engagement or knowledge exchange.

4. Conservation

The programme also identifies conservation as a possible area of collections-related research.

Applicants may therefore develop research that examines the cultural, historical or interpretive dimensions of conservation and the ways in which preservation decisions affect how collections are understood and used.

5. Other Collections-Related Research

The examples provided by the programme are not intended to limit the scope of potential projects.

Research may cover other aspects of collections work provided that the project has a strong connection to participating collections and is grounded in appropriate arts and humanities approaches.

Core Research Themes

The CC-EE programme highlights three broad themes that proposed projects may address:

Belonging

Projects may explore questions around identity, community, place, heritage and people’s relationships with collections and cultural institutions.

Research under this theme could examine how collections represent communities, how people relate to cultural heritage, or how institutions contribute to people’s sense of belonging.

Resilience

Research may also consider resilience at individual, community, institutional, cultural or environmental levels.

Projects could investigate how collections document experiences of change, disruption or adaptation, or how collections institutions themselves contribute to resilient communities and cultural practices.

Ecologies

The programme also welcomes projects connected to ecologies.

This theme can provide opportunities for research into relationships between people, collections, landscapes, environments and wider ecological systems, using suitable arts and humanities approaches.

A proposal may fit within one or more of these themes.

Who Is the Call Looking For?

The current opportunity is primarily aimed at potential PhD supervisors and collaborative project partners, rather than individual students applying directly for a PhD.

There are two principal categories of people who can become involved.

Staff at Participating CC-EE Collections

Staff working at one of the participating CC-EE collections can propose to supervise a doctoral student from the collections-based side of the partnership.

Importantly, the programme states that a proposed collections-based supervisor does not need to hold a PhD in order to supervise a PhD student.

This provides an opportunity for experienced professionals working within collections institutions to contribute their practical, curatorial, conservation, learning or other specialist expertise to doctoral research.

Staff at UK Higher Education Institutions

Academics and other relevant staff based at a UK Higher Education Institution can also participate.

University-based applicants are expected to propose a collaboration involving at least two, or preferably more, participating collecting institutions.

The university and collection partners can therefore jointly develop a doctoral project that combines academic research expertise with direct access to collections and professional knowledge.

Collaboration Is Central to the Studentship

One of the defining features of this opportunity is its collaborative nature.

A successful PhD project will not simply be a conventional university-based doctorate. Instead, it will bring together:

  1. A UK university;
  2. At least two CC-EE collecting institutions;
  3. Academic supervisors;
  4. Collections-based supervisors; and
  5. A doctoral researcher.

This model creates opportunities for research to move between academic and professional environments.

Applicants should therefore consider not only whether they have an interesting research idea, but also whether the proposed project can benefit from collaboration between multiple collections.

The programme particularly encourages projects involving more than the minimum two collecting institutions where this strengthens the research.

Support for Supervisors

The CC-EE team recognises that some prospective supervisors may have limited experience with collaborative doctoral supervision.

As a result, training and support are available for people who are new to supervising PhD students.

This is significant for collections professionals who may have extensive expertise in their specialist field but limited previous experience of doctoral supervision.

The programme provides an opportunity to develop supervisory experience while contributing to a substantial research project.

Support Available to Successful PhD Students

Students selected through the resulting doctoral opportunities will receive access to several forms of support.

Consortium Training

Students will have access to training delivered by the Consortium.

This is intended to complement their doctoral research and provide additional skills and knowledge beyond their individual institutional programme.

UK-Wide Collaborative Doctoral Programme Training

Students will also have access to training provided through the UK-wide Collaborative Doctoral Programme scheme.

This gives successful doctoral researchers an opportunity to participate in broader collaborative doctoral training and engage with researchers and institutions beyond their immediate project.

Dedicated Research Funds

The studentships will also provide students with dedicated research funds.

These resources can support the practical requirements of undertaking doctoral research and enable students to develop their projects using the collections and institutional partnerships on which their research is based.

Two-Stage Selection Process

The CC-EE studentship proposal process consists of two stages.

This means prospective supervisors should not wait until the final full application deadline before engaging with the programme.

Stage One: Expression of Interest

The first stage requires applicants to submit an Expression of Interest (EOI).

The deadline is:

26 October 2026 at 12:00 noon

Applicants who are interested in proposing a doctoral project are strongly encouraged to contact the CC-EE team before submitting the EOI.

The team can discuss the proposed research, provide guidance on developing the project and, where necessary, help connect applicants with relevant collection institutions.

Stage Two: Full Application

Applicants whose Expressions of Interest are successful will be invited to submit a full application.

The deadline for the full application is:

16 December 2026 at 12:00 noon

The full application stage provides an opportunity to develop the proposed project in greater depth following the initial assessment.

Applicants Are Strongly Encouraged to Contact the CC-EE Team

The programme strongly recommends that interested prospective supervisors communicate with the CC-EE team before submitting an Expression of Interest.

This preliminary discussion can be particularly useful when an applicant has a research idea but has not yet established all of the necessary institutional partnerships.

The CC-EE team can:

  • Discuss the proposed doctoral research idea.
  • Provide support in developing the proposal.
  • Help applicants understand the requirements of the programme.
  • Introduce applicants to relevant colleagues within participating collections.
  • Support the development of collaborative relationships.
  • Provide training and support for people who are new to PhD supervision.

Applicants should also discuss their proposed project with relevant staff at the collection institution or institutions on which the PhD would be focused.

The programme’s collaborative structure makes early communication particularly important.

How to Develop a Strong Proposal

Prospective applicants should consider several factors when developing an Expression of Interest.

Establish a Clear Research Question

The project should have a clear and meaningful research question that can be investigated through the collections involved.

The proposed research should go beyond simply describing a collection. It should demonstrate why the collections provide valuable evidence or material for answering the proposed research question.

Demonstrate the Value of the Collections

Applicants should clearly explain how the participating collections contribute to the research.

Where multiple collections are involved, the proposal should demonstrate why bringing them together adds value to the project.

Build Genuine Institutional Collaboration

Because collaboration is a central requirement, applicants should identify suitable collection partners and discuss the project with them early.

A successful project should establish a meaningful relationship between the university and participating collection institutions.

Connect With the Programme Themes

Applicants should consider whether their research can contribute to one or more of the programme’s themes:

  • Belonging
  • Resilience
  • Ecologies

Where relevant, the proposal should explain how the research contributes to these broader areas.

Use Arts and Humanities Methodologies

The programme specifically requires the research to use arts and humanities methods.

Applicants should therefore ensure that the methodology is appropriate to the nature of the research question and collections being investigated.

Expression of Interest Form

Applicants who wish to participate in the first stage must complete the official Expression of Interest form.

The form is available through the Collections & Communities in the East of England website.

The programme also provides information and support for prospective supervisors who are considering developing a proposal.

Expression of Interest deadline: 26 October 2026 at 12:00 noon.

Town Hall Information Session

The CC-EE programme also provided a Town Hall session for prospective applicants.

The session was scheduled for Thursday, 10 September at 2:00 pm and was intended to provide additional information about the studentship proposal process.

The programme states that the session would be recorded and added to the relevant webpage, allowing interested applicants to access the information afterwards.

Prospective applicants should consult the official programme page for the latest availability of the recording and any updated guidance.

Application and Preparation Timeline

Prospective supervisors can use the following timeline to organise their application:

Before 26 October 2026

  • Develop an initial doctoral research idea.
  • Identify relevant collections.
  • Contact potential collection partners.
  • Discuss the proposed project with the CC-EE team.
  • Consider how the research relates to belonging, resilience and/or ecologies.
  • Ensure that the proposed methodology is grounded in the arts and humanities.
  • Develop and submit the Expression of Interest.

26 October 2026 at 12:00 noon

Expression of Interest deadline.

Only proposals progressing through the first stage will move forward to the full application stage.

Between the EOI and Full Application Stages

Successful applicants can further develop their proposals and strengthen the collaboration between the university and collection partners.

This stage can be used to refine:

  • The research question;
  • Research methodology;
  • Collection access;
  • Supervisory arrangements;
  • Institutional responsibilities;
  • Project outcomes; and
  • The relationship between the participating collections.

16 December 2026 at 12:00 noon

Full Application deadline.

Successful full applications will contribute to the selection of doctoral projects for the 2027/28 studentships.

October 2027

The resulting PhD studentships are expected to begin.

Who Should Consider This Opportunity?

This opportunity is particularly relevant to people who already work with, research or have specialist knowledge of collections and who would like to develop that expertise into a collaborative doctoral project.

Potential participants include:

  • Staff working at participating museums and collecting institutions.
  • Curators interested in doctoral research.
  • Collections professionals.
  • Museum and heritage specialists.
  • Conservation professionals.
  • Learning and interpretation specialists.
  • Researchers working with cultural collections.
  • Academics based at UK universities.
  • Researchers in arts and humanities disciplines.
  • University staff seeking collaborative PhD projects with cultural institutions.
  • Experienced collections professionals interested in PhD supervision.
  • Potential supervisors seeking training and support in doctoral supervision.

The current call is not primarily a direct scholarship application for individual students. Instead, it is a call for the development of PhD projects and supervisory collaborations that will subsequently lead to externally advertised studentships.

Geographical Eligibility and Participation

The programme is focused on collections in the East of England, particularly participating institutions located in or associated with:

  • Cambridge
  • Norfolk
  • Colchester
  • Ipswich
  • Peterborough

University-based collaborators must be based at a UK Higher Education Institution.

For collections-based supervisors, participation is tied to the participating CC-EE collections.

The opportunity is therefore not presented as a general worldwide individual PhD scholarship open directly to applicants from every country. International researchers who are interested in the eventual PhD studentships should monitor the external advertisements when the individual studentship opportunities are announced, as the current proposal call is aimed at supervisors and institutional partners.

Why Collections-Based Doctoral Research Matters

Collections can provide researchers with access to primary materials that can illuminate questions that cannot always be answered through conventional academic sources alone.

Objects, documents, artworks, photographs, archives and other forms of collected material can offer evidence about communities, societies, historical events, cultural practices, environments and changing relationships between people and places.

A collaborative doctoral model can further strengthen this research by allowing a student to work across multiple collections.

For example, collections held in different locations may contain complementary materials relating to the same historical, cultural or social question. Bringing those resources together can create opportunities for comparative research and new interpretations.

The partnership can also allow doctoral researchers to engage with professionals who have specialist knowledge of the collections, their histories, cataloguing, preservation and public interpretation.

Benefits of the Collaborative Model

The CC-EE approach can provide several dimensions of professional and academic development.

For Universities

Universities can develop new doctoral research partnerships with cultural and collecting institutions and give doctoral students access to collections and specialist professional knowledge.

For Collections Institutions

Museums and other collections can contribute their expertise to doctoral research while developing new research relationships with universities.

For Supervisors

Supervisors can work across academic and collections environments, with training and support available to those who are new to doctoral supervision.

For Doctoral Students

Students selected through the resulting projects can gain:

  • Access to participating collections.
  • Collaborative supervisory support.
  • Consortium training.
  • UK-wide Collaborative Doctoral Programme training.
  • Dedicated research funds.
  • Experience working across academic and cultural institutions.
  • Opportunities to develop specialist research expertise.

How to Apply

Interested prospective supervisors should begin by discussing their research idea with the CC-EE team and relevant staff at the collection institutions they would like to involve.

The programme strongly recommends this preliminary engagement before the Expression of Interest is submitted.

The Expression of Interest form can then be completed and submitted before the first-stage deadline.

Applicants who successfully progress through the EOI stage will be invited to prepare a full application for consideration at the second stage.

The resulting studentships will subsequently be advertised externally for prospective PhD students.

APPLY HERE

Important Deadlines

Applicants should keep the following dates in mind:

Expression of Interest: 26 October 2026 at 12:00 noon

Full Application: 16 December 2026 at 12:00 noon

Expected PhD start date: October 2027

Because the programme operates a two-stage selection process, prospective applicants should begin discussions with the CC-EE team and potential collection partners well before the Expression of Interest deadline.

Official Application Resources

Prospective applicants can access the official Expression of Interest Form 2026 through the Collections & Communities in the East of England programme.

They can also consult information about participating collections and further guidance for potential supervisors through the official programme resources.

Applicants are encouraged to rely on the official CC-EE information for the latest requirements, deadlines and application instructions.

Visit HERE to learn more about the Collections & Communities in the East of England Collaborative Doctoral Landscape Award 2027.

Conclusion

The Collections & Communities in the East of England Collaborative Doctoral Landscape Award 2027 provides a structured opportunity for UK university researchers and professionals working within participating collections to develop collaborative PhD projects based on significant collections across the East of England.

With five studentships planned for 2027/28, the programme seeks research projects that bring together two or more CC-EE collections and a UK university and use arts and humanities methodologies to investigate meaningful questions connected to areas such as belonging, resilience and ecologies.

The programme also offers substantial support for the eventual doctoral researchers, including consortium training, UK-wide Collaborative Doctoral Programme training and dedicated research funds. Importantly, support is also available to supervisors who are new to doctoral supervision.

Anyone interested in proposing a project should begin discussions with the CC-EE team and relevant collections as early as possible. The first key deadline is 26 October 2026 at 12:00 noon for Expressions of Interest, followed by the 16 December 2026 at 12:00 noon deadline for full applications for proposals that successfully pass the first stage.

For more global scholarship opportunities visit OFY HERE

item.content:encoded:
The 2027 Safety Ambassador Fellowship is an opportunity for journalists in the United States who are passionate about improving the safety and well-being of fellow journalists and strengthening safety practices within local newsrooms. The fellowship is organized by the International Women’s Media Foundation (IWMF) with support from Press Forward as part of an expanded effort to strengthen safety infrastructure for local journalism across the United States.

Through the fellowship, selected Safety Ambassadors will receive specialized knowledge, practical tools, mentoring, and experience in journalist safety. The program is designed to prepare participants to become trusted resources within their journalism communities and help local journalists and newsrooms respond to the increasingly complex physical, digital, and psychosocial risks associated with journalism.

The initiative forms part of the IWMF’s broader Newsroom Safety Across America program, which aims to train approximately 3,000 local journalists across the United States while helping small newsrooms develop and implement effective safety policies.

About the 2027 Safety Ambassador Fellowship

Journalists today face a wide range of risks while performing their professional responsibilities. These risks can include physical threats, online harassment and digital security challenges, as well as psychosocial pressures associated with reporting, particularly in difficult or high-risk environments.

The 2027 Safety Ambassador Fellowship seeks to help address these challenges by developing a network of journalists who have the knowledge and skills to support their peers.

Safety Ambassadors will receive training that provides a holistic understanding of journalist safety, including:

  • Physical safety risks
  • Digital and online security threats
  • Psychosocial safety concerns
  • Risk assessment and management
  • Safety planning for journalists and newsrooms
  • Approaches for communicating safety information to peers
  • Training and facilitation skills

The program is intended to create a sustainable network of safety-focused journalism professionals who can continue supporting their colleagues beyond the fellowship itself.

What Is the Newsroom Safety Across America Initiative?

The Safety Ambassador Fellowship is connected to the IWMF’s Newsroom Safety Across America initiative.

With support from Press Forward, the initiative is expanding its efforts to provide safety training to thousands of local journalists throughout the United States. It also seeks to assist small newsrooms in developing and implementing safety policies that can help protect their staff and strengthen their overall preparedness.

A central component of this work is the development of Safety Ambassadors.

Rather than limiting safety knowledge to a small number of specialists, the initiative aims to create journalists within local communities who can share safety expertise with colleagues and help establish stronger safety practices throughout the profession.

Role of a Safety Ambassador

Participants selected for the fellowship will be expected to develop into knowledgeable resources for journalists and newsrooms within their communities.

After successfully completing the program, Safety Ambassadors will be equipped to provide support and share their knowledge with other journalism professionals.

Their expected activities include:

1. Delivering Safety Workshops

Safety Ambassadors will be prepared to deliver both virtual and in-person workshops covering relevant areas of journalist safety expertise.

These workshops can help journalists better understand the risks associated with their work and learn practical approaches to managing those risks.

The ability to deliver training is therefore an important component of the fellowship.

2. Supporting Fellow Journalists

Ambassadors will serve as resources for their peers within the journalism profession.

By sharing knowledge gained through the program, they can contribute to stronger safety awareness among journalists and help colleagues navigate physical, digital, and psychosocial safety challenges.

3. Supporting Future Safety Ambassadors

The fellowship is designed to create a continuing network of safety professionals within journalism.

Successful participants will therefore have opportunities to contribute to future cohorts of Safety Ambassadors by sharing their experience and expertise.

4. Representing the IWMF at Industry Events

Safety Ambassadors may also be featured by the IWMF at journalism conferences, trainings, and other industry events.

This provides participants with opportunities to contribute to broader conversations about journalist safety and share their expertise with professional audiences.

Benefits of the 2027 Safety Ambassador Fellowship

The fellowship offers participants several forms of professional development and support.

Individualized Mentoring

Fellows will receive individualized mentoring and advice from leading experts in journalism safety.

This mentorship can provide participants with an opportunity to strengthen their understanding of safety issues while learning from professionals with experience in the field.

Stipend

Participants will receive a small stipend intended to support their participation in the fellowship program.

The stipend provides financial assistance during the six-month commitment period.

Potential Paid Opportunities

Following successful completion of the fellowship, participants may have access to potential paid opportunities with the IWMF and its partners.

These opportunities are subject to availability and successful completion of the program and therefore should not be interpreted as guaranteed employment.

Professional Development

The fellowship provides participants with specialized knowledge in journalist safety, risk assessment, training, and peer support.

For journalists interested in newsroom leadership, professional development, journalist wellbeing, digital security, physical safety, or journalism capacity building, these skills can complement their existing professional experience.

Opportunity to Build a Professional Network

Participants will become part of a cohort focused on improving journalist safety.

The experience can facilitate professional connections with other journalists, safety experts, trainers, and organizations working to strengthen journalism safety.

Fellowship Commitment

The 2027 Safety Ambassador Fellowship requires a meaningful time commitment from selected participants.

Fellows must be willing to commit 10 hours per month over a six-month period.

This means applicants should consider whether they can consistently dedicate time to training, mentoring, learning, and other fellowship-related activities before applying.

Participants must also commit to delivering four training sessions after successfully completing the program.

The training requirement is an important component of the fellowship because the program is designed not only to develop individual expertise but also to create journalists who can share safety knowledge with their wider professional communities.

Who Should Consider Applying?

The fellowship is intended for people already working in journalism who have a strong interest in helping make journalism safer.

Potential applicants may include journalists working in local newsrooms and other journalism professionals who are interested in developing their expertise in safety and becoming trainers or resources for their peers.

Applicants should particularly consider the opportunity if they:

  • Work professionally in journalism.
  • Have a strong interest in journalist safety.
  • Want to help colleagues understand and manage safety risks.
  • Are interested in teaching or training other journalists.
  • Are willing to learn from safety experts.
  • Can dedicate approximately 10 hours each month for six months.
  • Are prepared to deliver four training sessions after completing the program.
  • Want to contribute to stronger safety practices within local newsrooms.
  • Are interested in physical, digital, and psychosocial safety issues affecting journalists.

Diversity and Geographic Representation

The IWMF states that it seeks diversity of lived experiences as well as geographic diversity within the Safety Ambassador program.

This means the fellowship is intended to build a cohort that reflects a variety of experiences and geographic communities within the United States.

The program is also open to journalists of all genders.

About the International Women’s Media Foundation

The International Women’s Media Foundation (IWMF) is an organization that works to support journalists and strengthen journalism safety.

The foundation describes itself as a leading provider of identity-informed and holistic safety training and resources for journalists and newsrooms, with a particular focus on women and nonbinary reporters in the United States and globally.

Through its safety work, the IWMF has trained thousands of journalists to strengthen their safety both online and offline.

The Safety Ambassador Fellowship builds on this broader body of work by developing journalists who can extend safety knowledge within their own professional communities.

Why Journalist Safety Training Matters

The risks faced by journalists are not limited to what happens while reporting in the field.

Modern journalism can expose professionals to multiple categories of risk simultaneously.

Physical Safety

Journalists may encounter physical risks while covering protests, conflicts, disasters, crime, political events, public demonstrations, or other potentially dangerous situations.

Understanding risk assessment and appropriate safety procedures can help journalists prepare more effectively for these assignments.

Digital Safety

Journalists increasingly depend on digital systems for communication, research, publishing, source management, and collaboration.

Digital threats can therefore affect both individual journalists and entire newsrooms.

Developing knowledge of digital safety can help journalists understand potential vulnerabilities and adopt stronger practices.

Psychosocial Safety

Journalism can also involve exposure to traumatic events, harassment, threats, intense workloads, and other pressures.

A holistic approach to safety therefore needs to consider psychosocial wellbeing alongside physical and digital security.

The Safety Ambassador Fellowship specifically emphasizes this broader understanding of journalist safety.

What Successful Participants Will Be Expected to Do

The fellowship is not simply a training opportunity. Participants are expected to use what they learn to benefit the wider journalism community.

Successful participants will therefore need to be prepared to:

  1. Participate actively in the six-month fellowship.
  2. Dedicate approximately 10 hours per month to the program.
  3. Develop their understanding of journalist safety and risk assessment.
  4. Learn from experienced journalism safety professionals.
  5. Share relevant safety knowledge with colleagues.
  6. Complete the fellowship successfully.
  7. Deliver four training sessions after completing the program.
  8. Contribute to the broader Safety Ambassador community where appropriate.

Applicants should therefore demonstrate not only an interest in learning but also a willingness to teach and support others.

Application Deadline

The application deadline for the 2027 Safety Ambassador Fellowship is Tuesday, October 20, 2026, at 7:00 AM.

Applicants should ensure that they submit their applications before the stated deadline. It is advisable to begin preparing the required application information well in advance rather than waiting until the final hours.

APPLY HERE

How to Prepare for the Application

Applicants can strengthen their preparation by reflecting on their professional experience and interest in journalist safety.

Before applying, prospective candidates should consider the following:

Demonstrate Your Journalism Experience

Applicants should clearly communicate their current involvement in journalism and explain the nature of their professional work.

Explain Your Interest in Safety

A strong application should clearly communicate why journalist safety matters to the applicant and why they want to develop expertise in this area.

Highlight Teaching and Training Potential

Because Safety Ambassadors will ultimately deliver training sessions, applicants should be prepared to demonstrate an interest in teaching, mentoring, facilitating workshops, or sharing professional knowledge.

Previous experience conducting workshops, training colleagues, speaking at professional events, mentoring journalists, or leading learning activities may be relevant.

Consider Your Availability

Applicants must be able to commit approximately 10 hours each month for six months.

They should therefore make sure they can accommodate the fellowship alongside their existing professional responsibilities.

Think About Your Local Journalism Community

The fellowship is intended to strengthen safety within journalism communities, particularly local newsrooms.

Applicants should consider how the knowledge and skills gained through the fellowship could be shared with colleagues and other journalists in their communities.

Visit HERE for more information about the 2027 Safety Ambassador Fellowship.

Conclusion

The 2027 Safety Ambassador Fellowship provides an opportunity for U.S.-based journalists to develop specialized expertise in journalist safety and become resources for their professional communities.

Supported by Press Forward and implemented through the International Women’s Media Foundation’s broader Newsroom Safety Across America initiative, the fellowship focuses on developing a network of Safety Ambassadors capable of understanding and addressing physical, digital, and psychosocial risks facing journalists and newsrooms.

Participants will receive individualized mentoring from journalism safety experts, a small participation stipend, and potential access to paid opportunities with the IWMF and its partners following successful completion. They will also gain the knowledge and tools needed to conduct safety workshops and support fellow journalists.

The program requires a commitment of 10 hours per month for six months, followed by a commitment to deliver four training sessions after successful completion.

For journalists based in the United States who are passionate about improving safety within the profession and are interested in learning, teaching, and supporting their peers, the 2027 Safety Ambassador Fellowship offers a structured pathway to develop these capabilities and contribute to stronger safety practices across local journalism communities.

For more global Fellowship opportunities, visit OFY HERE.
